solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cheeky types people sit on?

blocks.note: Surface reading: impudent, lippy people, perhaps ones who get trodden on by others.
Setter's reading: the body parts called cheeks, which everyone sits on.

explanation.surface: Sassy people who end up being sat on, put firmly in their place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' pretends to mean impudent, but here it means made of cheeks, the fleshy kind below the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear cheeks are literally the seat of the human body, the part resting on any chair.

clue.text: Slow defender gets prize (not first)

indicators.note: Losing what comes first means the opening letter is removed from the word.

blocks.note: In football or hockey a back is a defending player.
A prize is an award; drop its opening A.

explanation.surface: A sluggish defender is somehow still handed a trophy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slow' reads as describing the defender, but it is the definition standing alone at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Backward can describe a pupil who is behind in learning, a dated synonym for being slow.

clue.text: Wrestling, one wins belt causing injury

indicators.note: Wrestling twists and throws bodies about, so the letters are thrown into a new order.

blocks.note: Eleven letters of fodder, used exactly.

explanation.surface: A wrestler takes the championship belt but gets hurt in the process.
explanation.walkthrough: The wrestling surface points to a ring injury; the answer is from another sport entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis elbow is a painful strain of the forearm tendons, a common repetitive sports injury.

clue.text: Done with program, right? Work too hard!

blocks.note: When something is done, it is over.
An EXE is an executable computer program, named for its file extension.
RT is a standard abbreviation for right.

explanation.surface: Someone finishes a coding job and asks whether they have been pushing themselves too much.
explanation.walkthrough: EXE is the file extension of a Windows executable program, and RT is the usual abbreviation for right.
explanation.definitionFit: To overexert oneself is to strain beyond one's limits, a direct synonym for toiling excessively.

clue.text: Informal sort of family lawyer

blocks.note: Your kin are your relatives.
A DA is a District Attorney, an American prosecuting lawyer.

explanation.surface: Describing a casual kind of family solicitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of family lawyer' reads as one phrase, but 'Informal sort of' is the definition and the rest is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinda is a colloquial spelling of 'kind of', used to mean somewhat or rather in casual speech.

clue.text: Head of Gucci adored wearing hand warmers

indicators.note: The head of something is its top, so only the opening letter is kept.

blocks.note: Its initial letter.
Adored means loved.

explanation.surface: The fashion house's chief was delighted to be seen in a pair of mittens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Gucci' reads as the firm's boss, but it only supplies one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hand warmers are gloves, so someone wearing them is gloved, an adjective formed from the garment.

clue.text: Beats in musical phrases

blocks.note: To lick an opponent is to defeat them soundly.
A lick is a short riff or figure played by a guitarist or jazz soloist.

explanation.surface: Describing the rhythms found within snatches of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beats' looks musical alongside 'musical phrases', but here it means defeats.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: slang for thrashing a rival, and jazz or rock jargon for short improvised riffs.

clue.text: Russian man typically fails to start vehicle

indicators.note: Failing to start means the beginning is missing, so the opening letter goes.

blocks.note: Ivan is the stereotypical Russian man's name; drop its initial I.

explanation.surface: A Russian driver whose car will not get going, as usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Typically' signals a representative example: Ivan is the archetypal Russian name.
explanation.definitionFit: A van is a covered motor vehicle for carrying goods, a basic example of the category.

clue.text: Stop talking and do a household chore

blocks.note: A speaker who runs out of words or forgets their lines on stage.
In British kitchens, wiping the washed dishes with a tea towel.

explanation.surface: An instruction to be quiet and help with the housework.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'drying up' means drying the washed dishes with a tea towel.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms: falling silent on stage, and drying crockery after washing-up in a British kitchen.

clue.text: Old crack oddball found on base of box

indicators.note: In a down clue, sitting on the base puts one part directly beneath the other.

blocks.note: A chest is a large box.
An eccentric person is a nut.

explanation.surface: An eccentric with an old wisecrack is discovered at the bottom of a box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' here is a joke or wisecrack, not a split.
explanation.definitionFit: A chestnut is a stale, often-repeated joke; a crack is a quip, so an old one fits.

clue.text: Sentence Tory and Democrat in hearing

indicators.note: What is in hearing is judged by the ear, so the sound matters rather than the spelling.

blocks.note: A Tory is a Con(servative), a Democrat a Dem; said together they match the answer, whose final N is silent.

explanation.surface: A Conservative and a Democrat hand down a sentence at a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con-Dem' was the nickname for the 2010 UK coalition of Conservatives and Liberal Democrats; the answer's silent N makes it a perfect match.
explanation.definitionFit: To sentence a convicted person is to condemn them to a punishment, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Cough, having picked up joint in London area

indicators.note: Something picked up is caught by the ear, like a signal, so we want a sound-alike.

blocks.note: A hack is a dry, rasping cough.
The knee is a joint; its sound is spelt differently here.

explanation.surface: Someone develops a cough after picking up a joint somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a cannabis cigarette, which suits the cough; it is a body joint.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackney is a borough in east London, so it is a named example of a district of the capital.

clue.text: Pasty idiot kidnaps British swimmer

indicators.note: Kidnapping takes a captive and holds it, so one part is held inside the other.

blocks.note: A pasty complexion is pale.
B is the abbreviation for British.
A fool is an ass.

explanation.surface: A pale fool abducts a British swimming champion.
explanation.walkthrough: A pasty in Britain is also a pastry, but here it is the adjective for pale skin.
explanation.definitionFit: The white bass is a North American freshwater fish; 'swimmer' is a crossword cover word for any fish.

clue.text: King Charles punched weakling? Fight!

indicators.note: A punch drives into its target, so one part goes inside the other.

blocks.note: A sap is a feeble or gullible person.
CR stands for Carolus Rex, Latin for King Charles.

explanation.surface: The monarch lashes out at a wimp, and a brawl breaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: CR is the royal cipher Carolus Rex, used on things made in the reign of King Charles.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap is informal British English for a scuffle or brawl, a synonym of fight.

clue.text: Those in charge of clowns arresting Ms Wrong

indicators.note: Something wrong is not in its proper state, so the letters are not in their proper order.

blocks.note: Eleven letters of fodder, spanning two words.

explanation.surface: Circus bosses detain a woman who is the female equivalent of Mr Wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ms Wrong' reads as a play on Mr Wrong, but 'arresting' is fodder, not a container indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringmaster presides over circus acts, including the clowns, as master of ceremonies in the ring.

clue.text: At one time rob First Lady on Rhode Island

blocks.note: RI is the postal abbreviation for the US state.
Eve was the first woman in Genesis.

explanation.surface: Long ago a president's wife was robbed while visiting a New England state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests a president's wife; in crosswords she is usually Eve. In an across clue 'on' puts her after RI.
explanation.definitionFit: Rieve is an archaic spelling of reave, meaning plunder, so 'at one time' flags the old usage.

clue.text: Duke into nitrogen-enriched fruit and nut wrap

indicators.note: Going into something means entering it, so one part sits inside another.
Something enriched has had an extra ingredient mixed into it.

blocks.note: A banana is a fruit.
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen, added inside the fruit.
D is the abbreviation for Duke.

explanation.surface: Recipe-like: a fertilised fruit and some nuts wrapped together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit and nut' looks like a chocolate bar; 'nut' is slang for the head, and the break comes after 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandanna is a large coloured kerchief tied around the head, and nut is slang for head.

clue.text: Bishop enduring severe criticism

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop.
Enduring means lasting.

explanation.surface: A clergyman putting up with harsh condemnation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enduring' reads as the bishop suffering, but it is an adjective meaning long-lived.
explanation.definitionFit: A blasting is a fierce verbal attack or dressing-down, from the verb blast meaning to condemn.

clue.text: A&R alter piece from Lulu and Gabriel?

indicators.note: Only a piece is taken, a single letter from the start of the word.

blocks.note: The two letters as printed.
To alter is to change.
The singer's name supplies its initial.

explanation.surface: A record company's artists and repertoire team reworks a song by the singers Lulu and Peter Gabriel.
explanation.walkthrough: A&R is the talent-spotting department of a record label; Lulu and Peter Gabriel are singers, but Gabriel is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabriel is one example of an archangel, a chief angel, hence the question mark for definition by example.

clue.text: Standards by Steps

blocks.note: Standards are yardsticks against which things are judged.
Steps taken to achieve something, as in taking action.

explanation.surface: Pop classics recorded by the band Steps.
explanation.walkthrough: Steps is a British pop group and 'standards' are classic songs, but both words are definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Measures means benchmarks or yardsticks, and also courses of action taken, as in 'drastic measures'.

clue.text: A rubbish essay summary

blocks.note: As printed.
BS is slang shorthand for nonsense.
A tract is a short treatise or pamphlet.

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on a poor précis of a piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essay summary' looks like one phrase, but 'essay' is wordplay and 'summary' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An abstract is a short summary at the head of an academic paper, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Male caught in bed with English philosopher

indicators.note: Being caught in something means being trapped inside it.

blocks.note: A cot is a small bed.
M is the abbreviation for male.
E is the abbreviation for English.

explanation.surface: A man is found in bed with a thinker from England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English philosopher' seems to be one phrase, but the philosopher is French.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Comte was the French thinker who founded positivism and coined the term sociology.

clue.text: One stitches up wise man cuddling wife

indicators.note: Cuddling wraps arms around someone, so one part is held inside the other.

blocks.note: A seer is a prophet or sage.
W is the abbreviation for wife.

explanation.surface: Someone framing others, while a sage embraces his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stitches up' suggests framing someone; literally it is sewing.
explanation.definitionFit: A sewer is a person who sews with needle and thread, pronounced to rhyme with 'lower', not the drain.

clue.text: Well-turned out as Sting

blocks.note: Neatly and stylishly dressed.
To feel a sharp stinging pain.

explanation.walkthrough: Sting is a well-known singer, which makes the surface look like a compliment on his clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart describes someone neatly dressed, and as a verb means to hurt with a sharp, burning pain.

clue.text: Song and dance in service is a gas

indicators.note: Being in something places one part inside the other.

blocks.note: The Royal Navy, one of the armed services.
A song and dance is a fuss, or ado.

explanation.surface: Singing and dancing during a church service is great fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is a gas' suggests a hoot; it is literal. 'Song and dance' is the British idiom for a needless fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: Radon is a radioactive noble gas, element 86, so it is one example of the class.

clue.text: US sees maths spelt incorrectly

indicators.note: Letters that are spelt incorrectly are out of their proper order.

blocks.note: Nine letters of fodder.

explanation.surface: America notices British 'maths' is misspelt, since it writes 'math'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US' pretends to be the United States; it is the pronoun us, ordinary people.
explanation.definitionFit: Us, meaning we ordinary people collectively, matches the common people or general public.

clue.text: Story about grasping Catholic gets acclaim

indicators.note: Turning about means facing the other way, so the word runs backwards.
To grasp is to hold tight, so one part is held within the other.

blocks.note: A story is a tale.
C is the abbreviation for Catholic.

explanation.surface: A tale about a greedy churchgoer wins praise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' here turns the story backwards rather than meaning 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Éclat means brilliant success or applause, borrowed from French, and so a synonym for public praise.

clue.text: A fellow arresting outlaw in desert

indicators.note: Arresting someone takes them into custody, so one part is held inside another.

blocks.note: As printed.
To outlaw something is to ban it.
A don is a university fellow.

explanation.surface: A man detains a bandit in the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' and 'desert' suggest a Western; outlaw is a verb and desert a verb too. A don is an Oxbridge college fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert someone is to leave them behind for good, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Get on a giraffe on vacation

indicators.note: Vacating means emptying, so the inside letters are cleared out and only the ends stay.

blocks.note: As printed.
Its first and last letters.

explanation.surface: Climb aboard a giraffe while on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' suggests a trip, but it means the word is emptied.
explanation.definitionFit: To get on is an idiom for growing older, which is what ageing means.

clue.text: We messed around with large hose etc.

indicators.note: Things messed around are jumbled up and out of order.

blocks.note: As printed.
As printed.

explanation.surface: People fooling about with a big garden hose, among other things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hose' looks like a garden hosepipe; it is stockings or tights.
explanation.definitionFit: Hose means stockings and tights, which are types of garment worn on the legs.

clue.text: Time our man Slormgorm finds Ms Right?

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time.
The man in question is he.
The setter's pseudonym; a setter may refer to themselves as one.

explanation.surface: The setter wonders if the moment has come to meet the perfect partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Slormgorm is the setter of this puzzle, so the name stands for the setter speaking as 'one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ms Right is the ideal romantic partner, the person you are destined for, which is what the idiom means.

clue.text: Part of nasty list shocked Barnet workers

indicators.note: Only part of the phrase is wanted, a run of letters lying inside it.

blocks.note: The letters run across all three words.

explanation.surface: Staff in the north London suburb of Barnet are appalled by a spiteful list.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet looks like the London borough; it is rhyming slang, Barnet Fair for hair. 'Shocked' also hints at shocked hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair stylists work on people's hair, and in Cockney rhyming slang a barnet is a head of hair.
